disease_label_per_paper: Carbapenem-resistant Klebsiella pneumoniae catheter-associated urinary tract infection
presentation_summary: 66-year-old woman with an indwelling urethral catheter was hospitalized with persistent fever for 19 days after surgery for suppurative appendicitis.
Past history included sicca syndrome, cerebral infarction, and hypertension.
The urinary catheter initially could not be definitively removed because repeated removal attempts were followed by urinary retention.
During the CAUTI course she developed septic shock after catheter removal; urine and blood cultures later grew carbapenem-resistant Klebsiella pneumoniae.
Persistent catheter dependence and continuing CRKP urine cultures prompted a source-control strategy using intermittent catheterization plus rehabilitation to restore autonomous urination.

clinical_course: Oral fosfomycin ambutritol was started after admission and fever/CRP initially decreased.
Catheter removal on hospital day 8 was followed by septic shock requiring ICU-level support.
Tigecycline and polymyxin B were used after CRKP was identified in blood and urine cultures.
Blood cultures cleared after 2 days, but urine cultures continued to grow CRKP.
Polymyxin B was stopped after high-level resistance was detected and oral SMZco was started.
Because catheter removal attempts failed due to urinary retention, intermittent catheterization, acupuncture, pelvic floor muscle training, hydration planning, and voiding rehabilitation were used.
After 11 days of rehabilitation, the catheter was removed and autonomous urination was achieved.
actual_treatment: fosfomycin ambutritol 3 g daily early after admission
polymyxin B 50wu every 12 hours until resistance was detected
catheter-tip culture surveillance during intermittent catheterization
Crede manual pressure method after catheter removal

outcome.source_text_value: patient voided successfully, was discharged 3 days after catheter removal, and routine urinalyses stayed normal at 4-month follow-up

quality_warnings: CRKP species, KPC confirmation, susceptibility, blood culture identity, catheter-tip cultures, and treatment response are preserved as non-ranking confirmatory/treatment-context evidence.
The rankable snapshot focuses on catheter context, fever, urinary retention/source-control failure, urinalysis, and septic shock physiology.
